intro: Plain Modbus TCP lets anyone on the network read and write. Modbus/TCP Security wraps the same frames in TLS, on port 802. Both sides prove who they are with certificates, and the client's certificate can carry a role. The server's rules then decide, request by request, what that role may do.

connect.title: Connect
connect.text: The monitoring server opens TCP to the inverter on port 802, the port for Modbus/TCP Security. Port 502 can stay closed.

hello.title: Hello
hello.text: The client offers TLS 1.2 and one cipher suite. The inverter answers with its certificate and asks for the client's. Both sides must prove who they are: the specification requires it.

prove.title: Show the role
prove.text: The client sends its certificate. In it is a role, "Viewer", in an extension the Modbus Organization defined. The inverter checks the certificate against the CA it trusts and keeps the role for this connection.

read.title: Read: allowed
read.text: Now ordinary Modbus TCP frames travel inside encrypted TLS records. The inverter checks each request against its rules: a viewer may read. It answers 4820.5 kW.

write.title: Write: refused
write.text: The client tries to set a power limit. A viewer may not write, so the inverter refuses with exception 01, the code the specification sets for this. The limit stays at 5000 kW.

frames.tcp: Open a TCP connection to port 802
frames.client-hello: Let's talk TLS 1.2, with this cipher suite
frames.server-hello: Here is my certificate. Show me yours.
frames.client-cert: Here is mine, role Viewer, and proof that it is mine
frames.write-req: (encrypted) Set the power limit to 3000 kW

notes.tcp: Plain TCP to port 802, not 502. Only the TLS handshake follows in clear.
notes.server-hello: Five handshake messages. ServerHello picks TLS 1.2 and 0xC02F. Certificate carries the inverter's certificate and its CA's. ServerKeyExchange holds the inverter's half of the key exchange, signed with its key. CertificateRequest asks for the client's certificate: a Modbus/TCP Security server must always ask. ServerHelloDone ends its turn.
notes.client-cert: Certificate carries the client's certificate, with the role. ClientKeyExchange holds the client's half of the key exchange. CertificateVerify signs the handshake so far: proof that the client holds the certificate's private key. ChangeCipherSpec and Finished turn encryption on. In TLS 1.2 the certificates travel in clear, so anyone on the network can read the role.
notes.server-finished: The inverter turns encryption on too. Had the client sent no certificate, or one from an unknown CA, the inverter would have ended the connection with an alert.

rec-handshake.name: Record type 22
rec-handshake.note: 0x16: a handshake record. The handshake travels in clear.

rec-v10.name: Record version
rec-v10.note: 0x0301. Clients write this old number here so that old servers do not choke. The version they want comes a few bytes later.

hello-version.name: Version
hello-version.note: 0x0303: TLS 1.2. Modbus/TCP Security needs 1.2 or newer.

random.name: Random
random.note: 32 random bytes, shown 8 at a time. Both sides mix them into the session keys.

session-id.name: Session ID
session-id.note: Length 0: a new session, not a resumed one.

suites.name: Cipher suites
suites.note: 2 bytes, one suite: 0xC02F, key exchange with ECDHE, RSA certificates, AES-128-GCM encryption, SHA-256. The specification requires it for devices with RSA keys.

ext-reneg.name: renegotiation_info
ext-reneg.note: 0xFF01, empty: the client supports safe renegotiation, which the specification requires.

ext-points.name: ec_point_formats
ext-points.note: 0x000B: how elliptic-curve points may be written.

ext-groups.name: supported_groups
ext-groups.note: 0x000A, 12 bytes: a list of 10 bytes follows.

groups.name: Curves
groups.note: Five curves for the key exchange: x25519 (0x001D), P-256 (0x0017), x448, P-384 and P-521. Every device that uses elliptic curves must support P-256.

ext-sigalgs.name: signature_algorithms
ext-sigalgs.note: 0x000D: a list of 40 bytes follows, 2 for each of 20 algorithms.

sigalgs.name: Signatures
sigalgs.note: Kinds of signature the client accepts, 2 bytes each. 0x0403 is ECDSA on P-256 with SHA-256; 0x0401, further on, is RSA with SHA-256.

sigalgs-more.name: Signatures
sigalgs-more.note: More kinds of signature, 2 bytes each.

rec-app.name: Record type 23
rec-app.note: 0x17: application data. What follows is encrypted.

len-read-req.name: Length
len-read-req.note: 36 bytes follow, not shown: an 8-byte nonce, the 12-byte request encrypted, and a 16-byte tag. Inside is the plain Modbus TCP request 00 01 00 00 00 06 01 03 00 64 00 02: read registers 100 and 101.

len-read-resp.name: Length
len-read-resp.note: 37 bytes follow: nonce, 13 bytes of answer, tag. Inside: 00 01 00 00 00 07 01 03 04 A4 00 45 96, active power 4820.5 kW.

len-write-req.name: Length
len-write-req.note: 36 bytes follow. Inside: 00 02 00 00 00 06 01 06 00 C8 0B B8, write 3000 to register 200, the power limit.

len-refused.name: Length
len-refused.note: 33 bytes follow: nonce, 9 bytes of answer, tag. Inside: 00 02 00 00 00 03 01 86 01. 0x86 is 0x06 with the error bit set; 01 is the exception code.

a-extension.name: Extension
a-extension.note: A SEQUENCE of 0x17 = 23 bytes: one extension of the certificate.

a-oid.name: Object ID
a-oid.note: 1.3.6.1.4.1.50316.802.1: the Modbus role. 50316 is the number IANA gave the Modbus Organization.

a-octets.name: Value
a-octets.note: An OCTET STRING of 8 bytes that holds the extension's value.

a-utf8.name: UTF8String
a-utf8.note: 0x0C: text in UTF-8, 6 bytes long. The specification requires this type.

a-role.name: Role
a-role.note: "Viewer". One role per certificate. The server's rules say what it may do.

facts.standard: MODBUS/TCP Security Protocol Specification (Modbus Organization, 2018, revised 2021)
facts.between: Client with a certificate → server with a certificate
facts.security: Both sides prove who they are with X.509 certificates. A role in the client's certificate decides what it may do.
facts.frames: The usual Modbus TCP frames, unchanged, inside TLS records

tips: A certificate without a role still connects. The server then applies its rules for "no role": make sure they allow nothing.
A refused request returns exception 01, the same code as an unknown function. Check the role and the rules before you hunt for a bug.
Each certificate holds exactly one role. A tool that must read and write needs one role that allows both.
Certificates expire. Plan how new ones reach every device before the first one runs out, or the plant stops talking on that day.

anatomy.role: The role extension in the client's certificate, byte by byte

playground.file: The monitoring server's certificate, as openssl x509 -text prints it. The role is the last extension.
playground.issuer: The CA that signed it. The inverter accepts only certificates from a CA it trusts.
playground.expiry: After this date the inverter refuses the certificate.
playground.subject: Whom the certificate belongs to: the monitoring server.
playground.client-auth: This certificate may be used by a TLS client.
playground.role-oid: The Modbus role extension. openssl does not know its name, so it prints the number.
playground.role-value: The role. The two dots are the bytes 0x0C and 0x06 (UTF8String, 6 characters), which openssl cannot print.
